Invective

/in-VEK-tiv/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Invective means a sharp, angry verbal attack; harsh, insulting language.

Invective means a sharp, angry verbal attack; harsh, insulting language. The coach was fined after unleashing a stream of invective at the officials' table.

Worked Example

The reservoir hearing opened with charts and careful questions. But when the vote went against the marina project, its lead investor seized the microphone. He called the commissioners frauds, sneered at the town engineer's degree, and questioned the honesty of everyone who had testified. Security finally cut the sound as the stream of invective showed no sign of slowing.

Calling the commissioners frauds and insulting everyone who testified is a sustained burst of harsh, insulting language — that verbal attack is what invective names.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — insult → vitriol → invective

insult vs. invective

insult vs. invective: An insult is weaker than invective: an insult is a single cutting remark, while invective is a sustained stream of them.

vitriol vs. invective

vitriol vs. invective: Vitriol is stronger than invective — vitriol suggests language so corrosively bitter it burns like acid, while invective can be loud and abusive without that concentrated cruelty.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of invective.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: against

Root — vect

Root — vect: to carry (Latin vehere, vectus)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to; having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Invective assembles neatly: in- ('against') + vect ('to carry', from vehere, the root of vehicle and convection) + -ive. Latin invectivus described speech 'carried against' someone — an attack delivered in words. One twist to notice: although -ive normally builds adjectives, invective has settled into English as a noun naming the attacking language itself, a reminder that -ive words occasionally drift into noun territory.

Use the root in a new word: convection

Use the root in a new word: convection: Warm air rises and cool air sinks in convection currents — vect, 'to carry,' the same root that makes invective an attack 'carried against' its target.
